title: India-UK Trade Deal Takes Effect, but Can It Avoid the Pitfalls of Past FTAs?
excerpt: The Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement brings tariff cuts, professional mobility gains, and a social security exemption for NRIs — but India's mixed track record with trade agreements looms over the landmark pact.
body:
• The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) came into force on July 15, 2026, marking India's first major bilateral trade deal with a developed Western economy.
  • Britain immediately eliminated tariffs on 96.8% of tariff lines, while India will phase out duties on 85% of British goods over ten years.
  • A Double Contribution Convention exempts Indian professionals from UK social security payments for up to five years, benefiting an estimated 75,000 workers.
  • Past FTAs with ASEAN, Japan, and South Korea yielded import surges rather than export gains — the question is whether the UK deal avoids the same pattern.

India's Most Comprehensive Trade Deal Takes Effect

The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement came into force on July 15, five days after its signing in July 2025, following over three years of negotiations that survived four British Prime Ministers and several missed deadlines. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal described it as "the most comprehensive agreement India has entered into so far" during UK-India Week in London.

The deal immediately opens significant market access on both sides. Britain eliminated tariffs on 96.8% of tariff lines — covering 97.7% of trade by value — on day one. India will remove duties on 64.1% of tariff lines immediately and phase out a further 21% over the coming decade, while shielding sensitive products including dairy, apples, and cheese.

For Indian exporters, the gains are concentrated in labour-intensive sectors. Tariffs on textiles, leather, footwear, marine products, gems and jewellery, and processed foods have been eliminated entirely. Engineering exports to Britain — already $4.7 billion in FY26 and growing at 34.4% year-over-year — are expected to benefit from improved access for electrical machinery, auto components, and steel.

"Every trading relationship and every partnership stands on its own legs. The UK Free Trade Agreement is going to be the most comprehensive agreement that India has entered into so far."

— Piyush Goyal, Commerce Minister, India

What Makes This Deal Different

Several provisions in the CETA break new ground for India's trade agreements. For the first time, India has opened its automobile sector to preferential imports, reducing tariffs from 100% to 10% on British luxury vehicles under a quota system allowing 37,000 fully built units annually. India has also opened approximately 40,000 high-value government procurement contracts to UK bidders — a strategic shift away from using public procurement exclusively for domestic industrial development.

The deal includes chapters on labour rights, environmental standards, anti-corruption, and gender equality — areas India has historically resisted including in trade agreements. These provisions, while largely aspirational, signal a willingness to align with international standards that will be closely watched in parallel negotiations with the United States and the European Union.

The services package expands market access across 137 sub-sectors, including IT, business services, telecommunications, finance, and education. It also eases temporary entry rules for business visitors, investors, and independent professionals — a priority for India's services-driven economy.

The Social Security Win for NRIs

Perhaps the most immediately consequential provision for the Indian diaspora is the linked Double Contribution Convention. The agreement exempts Indian professionals temporarily working in the UK from paying into Britain's National Insurance system for stays of up to five years, benefiting approximately 75,000 workers and 900 employers.

The convention is expected to generate savings of around 20% for Indian employers and total financial gains of ₹4,000 crore. For NRIs in the UK — one of the largest Indian diaspora communities globally — this eliminates the long-standing problem of paying into social security systems without qualifying for benefits.

The precedent matters beyond the UK. Indian professionals in the United States face a similar issue with H-1B and L-1 visa holders paying into Social Security without qualifying. The Hindu Business Line editorial noted that the UK social security agreement "decidedly works as a strong bargaining chip for India in its deliberations with the US."

Lessons From Past Agreements

The central question is whether the CETA will deliver results where India's previous trade agreements have not. FTAs with ASEAN, Japan, and South Korea led to import surges without proportionate export gains, as Indian companies struggled to penetrate partner markets due to stringent standards, non-tariff barriers, and domestic constraints in scaling up.

The UK deal's asymmetric structure — where Britain offers near-total immediate liberalisation while India phases in reductions over a decade — is designed to mitigate this risk. But the exclusion of the UK's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), set to take effect in January 2027, from the agreement leaves a significant unresolved issue. The CBAM would levy taxes on carbon-intensive Indian exports including iron, steel, and fertilisers, potentially eroding tariff gains.

"Past FTAs, whether with ASEAN, Japan or South Korea, have not yielded the expected dividends for Indian industry. The success of the CETA with UK will be determined by how it pans out on the ground."

— The Hindu Business Line Editorial

With bilateral trade currently at approximately £42 billion and a target of $120 billion by 2030, the scale of ambition is significant. India's new PM-designate inheriting the deal from Andy Burnham's government will need to ensure the implementation machinery matches the policy intent. For the 1.6 million-strong Indian diaspora in the UK, the deal's success will be measured not in tariff schedules but in jobs, investment flows, and the professional mobility it enables.
